title: Can This Vermont Company Remake the Electric Aviation Industry?
gist: Beta Technologies, one of the top three US electric aircraft makers, plans to certify the runway-based Alia CX300 first (expected 2027) and then reuse that evidence for the A250 eVTOL a year later, starting with cargo and medical missions before passengers. The company is vertically integrated across motors, batteries, avionics and an open CCS charging network (138 sites), and also supplies motors and software to Eve and Horizon. Battery weight remains the binding constraint on electric aviation.

insights.claim: Aviation catastrophic-failure conditions must generally be held to about one in a billion flight hours, which individual electrical components cannot meet alone. Electric aircraft therefore rely on layered redundancy such as duplicate power paths and independent inverters, each layer adding weight and complexity.

insights.claim: Beta's H500A pusher motor builds redundancy in by splitting inverters and stator sections, so it can lose half its system and still function the same. themes.theme: Talent and manufacturing base in Vermont

insights.claim: Beta employs about 1,500 people, mostly in South Burlington, Vermont, at a 17,500-square-meter facility. It recruits people who have vacationed or studied in Vermont and offers flying lessons, a health clinic and a planned day care to attract and keep talent in a small labor market.

insights.so_what: Lifestyle-based recruiting is how Beta scales headcount away from aerospace hubs.
